title: Baidu CEO Warns AI Needs Better Monetization to Avoid Bubble
summary: Robin Li says AI investments risk becoming a bubble without clear revenue gains. Baidu faces sixth straight quarterly drop as commercialization challenges
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Baidu CEO Robin Li warned that AI investments could become a bubble without better monetization and revenue gains.
- Baidu reported its sixth consecutive quarterly revenue decline, underscoring challenges in commercializing AI ventures despite early investments.
- Li called for organizational changes including breaking role boundaries and teaching AI unwritten company rules to accelerate adoption.


Baidu CEO Robin Li issued a stark warning about the future of artificial intelligence investments at the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen on November 17, 2026. Without clear monetization strategies and revenue growth, Li cautioned that AI could become a bubble rather than a transformative business tool. His comments come as Baidu reported its sixth consecutive quarterly revenue decline, highlighting the gap between AI development costs and commercial returns.


## The Monetization Urgency


Speaking at the summit, Li described the current state of AI development as "very urgent" and expressed disappointment with the pace of AI adoption across user-facing applications. The Baidu chief has been a long-time AI investor, committing resources to technologies like self-driving software years before ChatGPT sparked the current wave in 2022. Yet he sees a troubling pattern: companies are spending heavily on AI infrastructure and development without corresponding increases in sales or profit.


"Without a clear increase in revenue or profit for companies spending heavily on AI, the common fear that[AI is merely a bubble](https://emergent.sh/news/ai-bubble-warnings-vs-reality-wall-street) could well become a reality," Li stated. His concern centers on what he called "AI diffusion," the rate at which artificial intelligence technologies translate into practical business applications that generate revenue. For companies across industries, the promise of AI has not yet materialized into sustainable financial returns.


## Baidu's Commercial Challenges


Baidu's own financial performance underscores the monetization challenge Li highlighted. Officially released on November 16, 2026, the company's latest quarterly results showed a sixth straight revenue drop, with shares declining more than other leading Chinese internet companies. Part of the struggle stems from Baidu's less developed cloud infrastructure business compared to competitors like Tencent Holdings and Alibaba Group Holding.


However, Li noted one bright spot: graphics card rentals, which provide access to AI accelerators essential for training and inference work, now contribute a larger share of company profit. This service-based revenue stream represents the type of practical AI monetization Li believes the industry needs more of.


## Organizational Change Requirements


Beyond technology development, Li argued that companies must undergo fundamental organizational changes to successfully commercialize AI. He called for breaking down traditional occupational role boundaries and teaching AI systems the valuable but unwritten rules within companies about how work actually gets done. These cultural and structural shifts, Li suggested, are as important as technical capabilities for realizing AI's business potential.


The Baidu CEO emphasized that demand for AI exists, but understanding how to effectively deploy and monetize it takes time. "I am still optimistic as AI is an inevitable trend," he said. "It's not that there's a lack of AI demand, but rather it takes time for people to understand AI."


## What This Means


Li's warning reflects broader concerns about whether massive AI investments will deliver proportional returns. As one of China's earliest AI investors, Baidu's commercialization struggles serve as a cautionary example for the global AI industry. The gap between technological capability and business value creation remains wide, and without practical monetization strategies, investor enthusiasm could wane. For companies betting heavily on AI, Li's message is clear: technical innovation alone won't justify continued investment without demonstrable revenue growth and profit improvement.
